spots.s: Free 25-acre botanical garden plus the 150-acre Newman Arboretum and 3,500 acres of gorges and natural areas — the Nevin Welcome Center is the trailhead for all of it.

spots.n: Herbert F. Johnson Museum of Art
spots.s: I.M. Pei's concrete monolith on the Arts Quad rim — 40,000 works, free admission, and a fifth-floor gallery with a 360° view down Cayuga Lake.
Free visitor center at Sapsucker Woods with live bird cams, a two-story window on the pond, and four miles of boardwalk trails; open Tue–Sun 10–4, trails dawn to dusk.
Ice cream made a few feet away in Stocking Hall by the food-science department — the campus ritual, and the cheapest good thing on the hill.
215 feet in a single plunge — taller than Niagara and the tallest free-falling waterfall east of the Rockies. Flat 0.75-mi gorge trail to the base, or drive to the overlook.
Ten waterfalls stacked up a 0.75-mi gorge trail at the edge of the city, with a natural swimming hole at the bottom in summer.
Lucifer Falls drops 115 feet into a mile of stone-carved gorge trail; the lower park has the best swimming hole in the county, right below a waterfall.
150 feet wide, 100 feet tall, and a two-minute walk from the car — the easiest big waterfall in Ithaca, at the bottom of the Fall Creek gorge below campus.
Four car-free blocks of independent shops, patios, buskers and the State Theatre marquee — downtown's living room, ten minutes down the hill from campus.
21 bells rung live by student chimesmasters three times a day since 1868. Climb the 161 steps and watch from the chamber — no reservation, just show up.
A cast-iron, two-tier Victorian reading room inside Uris Library that looks like a film set — open to visitors when the library is, and worth the detour.
The Paleontological Research Institution's museum — a 44-foot right whale skeleton, a mastodon, and a genuinely good walk through deep time.
Hands-on science museum with a 250-piece outdoor Sagan Planet Walk that scales the solar system across downtown Ithaca.
Six miles of trails, a six-story treehouse and rescued local wildlife on a hillside above the lake — the PRI's outdoor half.
The south shore of Cayuga Lake: a restored 1890s carousel, huge lawns, the best swan-and-sunset walk in town, and the start of the Waterfront Trail.
Farm brewery on 12 acres south of town — Flower Power IPA on the source, a real kitchen, and lawn tables that stay full until frost.
The university's own orchard sells its apples, cider and cider donuts straight off the research plots on Route 366 — peak season is exactly when you'd be here.
Tasting room and 'Cider Bar' on a hill farm north of town pouring the region's best dry ciders, with a view over Cayuga that justifies the drive.
The closest winery to campus — ten minutes out Route 79, small tasting room, and a lawn that faces the vines at sunset.
The plunge pool at the base of Buttermilk's main cascade is a lifeguarded swimming area in summer — the single best free thing to do in Ithaca in August.
Nonprofit tour boat out of the Ithaca inlet — narrated lake ecology cruises, sunset trips, and a floating classroom you can just buy a ticket for.

spots.n: Allan H. Treman State Marine Park
spots.s: The largest inland marina in New York, at the lake's south end — boat launch, the Waterfront Trail, and the best flat sunset view over Cayuga.
One of the best college film programs in the country, in Willard Straight Hall — 35mm repertory, new international releases, and $5-ish student tickets.
Professional summer-and-fall theater in a converted airplane hangar by the lake, plus touring comedy, indie shows and circus nights.
A restored 1928 movie palace on West State St, 1,600 seats — the room that catches national touring acts on their way between cities.

events.s: Three days of cider, apple everything, 150 vendors and live music filling the Commons and the surrounding streets. Free.
Elton John tribute at the Hangar Theatre.
Stand-up at the State Theatre's 1,600-seat 1928 movie palace.
Homecoming at Schoellkopf Field — the tailgate on the Crescent starts hours before kickoff and the whole campus turns out.
North Country rival at Lynah on a Friday night in November — the Cornell hockey experience in its purest form.
Ivy League hockey at Lynah Rink, where the student section has a script and uses it.
ECAC opener at Lynah against the league's heavyweight — the hardest ticket of the fall.
Two nights of exhibition hockey at Lynah Rink to open the home season.
The Saturday half of the North Country weekend at Lynah Rink.
The first skate at Lynah — the exhibition where you find out what the team has, in the loudest small rink in college hockey.
Dan Bejar solo at the Hangar Theatre — a small room for a songwriter who usually plays bigger ones.
Independent pro wrestling in a theater, which is exactly as good as it sounds.
An evening of stories, sonnets and audience singalongs at the Hangar.
Up to 150 bands playing on the porches of the Fall Creek and Northside neighborhoods, free, all afternoon — the best day of the Ithaca year. Makers Market too.
The folk singer at the State Theatre, six decades into the catalogue.
Blues-rock guitarist and songwriter at the State Theatre, with Penelope Road opening.
Contemporary circus at the Hangar as part of the Hupstate festival — aerial and acrobatic work, one afternoon only.
The Icelandic indie-folk band at the State Theatre.

events.n: Steve Gonsalves: A Life With Ghosts
events.s: The Ghost Hunters investigator's touring show at the Hangar.
In Flight Entertainment's drag revue at the Hangar, hosted by Tilia Cordata.
A full-band live tribute to Fleetwood Mac at the Hangar.
Duluth string band at the State Theatre, with Wild Horses.
The Hangar's annual fundraiser quiz under the tent by the lake — teams, prizes, and a bar.
Vaudeville-and-sideshow variety night at the Hangar Theatre.

coffee.s: The classicists' cafe in Klarman Hall — soup, espresso and busts of Greek philosophers watching you write your paper. The most Cornell room on campus.
The architecture school's cafe in the basement of Sibley Hall — plywood, drafting refugees, and coffee served to people who have not slept.
Mann Library's independent cafe on the Ag Quad — local beans, real breakfast sandwiches, and the friendliest counter on campus.
Olin Library's ground-floor cafe, open late in term — where you go when the reading room wins and you need another hour.
Duffield Hall's atrium cafe under the glass roof — the engineering quad's meeting point and the easiest coffee on north-central campus.
In the Physical Sciences Building — espresso, bahn mi and a quiet upstairs table when Libe is full.
The Cornell Store's cafe in the Cornell Center — the default meet-someone-for-coffee spot on Ho Plaza.
The roaster that put Ithaca on the third-wave map in 2000 and now supplies half of New York. The North Cayuga St shop is the original bar.
CTB since 1976 — the bagel, the coffee and the 7am line that every Cornell generation has stood in. The College Ave store is the Collegetown one.
Sun-filled minimalist cafe in Press Bay Alley behind the Commons — the quietest good coffee downtown and a fine place to actually work.
Ithaca-roasted beans poured at their own bar — heavier, darker profile than Gimme, and the local's counter-argument.
Roaster, bottle shop and cafe in one — the Press Bay location does espresso and a serious beer wall from the same counter.
Collegetown's coffee-by-day, cocktails-by-night hybrid — the rare Collegetown room that works for a first date and a 9am espresso alike.
The Meadow St mothership of the CTB family — full bakery counter, deli, and the biggest coffee-and-a-sandwich operation in town.

eats.s: The 1973 collective that wrote the vegetarian cookbook your parents own — still a co-op, still changing the menu daily, still worth going once.
Spanish-leaning small plates and a 100-bottle-by-the-glass list on a Commons side street — the best date-night table downtown, and it has been for 30 years.
The county college's culinary program running a real downtown bistro — wood-fired, sourced from their own farm, and better than that description sounds.
The tonkotsu bowl Cornell students actually queue for — thin noodles, long-cooked broth, and a small room that fills by 6.
Collegetown's sushi standby — a long nigiri list, a quiet minimalist room, and the closest decent raw fish to campus.
Small Collegetown sushi bar doing chirashi and omakase-ish specials better than its storefront suggests.
High-end pan-Asian small plates on the Commons — the pork buns and the sushi list are the reason, the cocktail program is the surprise.
The Commons' anchor restaurant, rebuilt after a truck drove through it — long bar, raw bar, and the best people-watching window in Ithaca.
Big burgers, 20 taps and a room loud enough to bring a group to — downtown's dependable Friday.
Blistered NY-style pies and a proper Caesar in a bright downtown room — the pizza locals name first.
Arepas, tacos and a mezcal list at two locations (Collegetown and downtown) — fast, cheap and genuinely good.
Commons-corner Mexican with a big margarita program and a patio that runs late — the default group dinner.
Pho and bun cha done properly, a short walk off the Commons — Ithaca's best cheap dinner when it's cold.
The counter-service half of Ithaca's Thai institution — fast, fiery, and open when Collegetown gets out.
Thirty-plus years of Lebanese-leaning plates on the Commons — the vegetarian-friendly option that isn't Moosewood.
The Pinesburger on English muffin bread, eaten in a wood-panelled roadhouse above Cayuga Lake — an Ithaca rite of passage.
Making ice cream in Ithaca since 1936 — the counter, the sundaes, and the line out the door every warm evening.
A lunch wagon that has parked near campus since 1918 — late-night subs and dogs, cash-friendly, an actual piece of Cornell history.
Fall Creek's corner restaurant — fried chicken, a fireplace, and the neighborhood table that isn't downtown or Collegetown.
Big Irish room off the Commons — a fireplace, a whiskey list, and where the graduate students end up.
Seasonal, ambitious plates in a small downtown dining room — the reservation to make when someone visits.
Collegetown Indian with a lunch buffet that has fed generations of Cornell students, and a curry list that holds up at dinner.
The pavilion's international food stalls — Cambodian, Ethiopian, Vietnamese, wood-fired pizza — eaten at picnic tables over the water.

nightlife.s: Stewart Ave legend rebuilt after the 2019 fire — a deep tap list, wooden booths, and professors drinking next to lifers and students.
The basement dance floor under College Ave — Collegetown's actual club, hip-hop-heavy and packed after midnight on a Thursday.
Dryden Rd's patio bar — the summer and early-fall Collegetown default when nobody wants to be inside yet.
The Collegetown dive, unchanged and unbothered — cheap pitchers, a jukebox, and the bar every Cornell alum asks about.
The Argos Inn's bar: antique furniture, a chandelier, serious cocktails, and a Carriagehouse patio out back in warm months. Jazz on Wednesdays.
The Argos annex, Thursday through Saturday — DJs, dancing and a room that runs later than the rest of downtown.
The Commons' live-music room — local bands most nights, a real stage, and a bar you can still hear yourself at between sets.
Minimalist inlet-side venue with the best sound system in the county, booking touring indie, jam and hip-hop acts.
Small, dark, deliberate cocktail bar downtown — the grown-up drink after dinner on the Commons.
Inlet-side taproom with a garage-door wall, rotating sours and IPAs, and food trucks parked outside most nights.
Small, sharp brewery on the west end — clean lagers, a patio, and a quieter alternative to the Ithaca Beer lawn.
Late tequila bar off the Commons where the dance floor opens up after 11 on weekends.
The Statler Hotel's bar on campus — run in part by hotel-school students, with a terrace that looks straight down the lake at sunset.
'The Rongo' — a resurrected 1970s roadhouse 12 miles up the lake, live music, and the county's most beloved bar-in-a-village.

sights.s: The lawn below the Arts Quad falls away toward the lake — the whole west side of campus sits on it at 7pm in September, and it earns the reputation.
The oldest quad on campus: Morrill, McGraw and White halls in 1860s stone, plus the two statues students argue about at midnight.
Cornell's nondenominational chapel — Tiffany-era glass, a painted ceiling, and Ezra Cornell's tomb in the apse. Free, usually open, almost always empty.
OMA's 2011 slab hanging unsupported over University Ave — the most argued-about building on campus, best seen from the sidewalk underneath.
A swaying 1960s footbridge 140 feet above the Fall Creek gorge — the shortest walk on campus that will make your stomach drop.
The falls and stone dam at the west end of Beebe Lake, right on campus — thirty seconds off the path between north and central campus.
The high point of the Newman Arboretum: a bench, a stand of conifers, and the best foliage view of the whole valley in mid-October.
Drive-up platform at the gorge rim — the postcard shot of a 215-foot fall with no hiking at all, five minutes off Route 89.
A 40-foot ledge on Six Mile Creek behind the Van Natta dam, minutes from downtown and known mostly to locals.
The 1878 octagonal-roofed carriage house that is now the graduate student center — and the nicest porch on campus.
A 1.2-billion-to-1 scale model of the solar system laid across downtown Ithaca, from the Commons to the Sciencenter, in memory of Carl Sagan.
The engineered wetland garden below the Nevin Center — an unglamorous idea done beautifully, and full of birds at dusk.

walks.s: The stone staircase that connects campus to downtown past nine waterfalls — a 20-minute walk that is the single best thing about living on this hill. Closed in winter.
From the suspension bridge down along the north rim to Ithaca Falls — campus's other gorge, steeper and emptier than Cascadilla.
A 1.2-mile flat loop around the campus lake, past Triphammer Falls and the Sackett footbridge — the run or think-walk you'll do most often.
Six flat, paved miles from Stewart Park around the inlet to Cass Park — walk it, run it or ride it; the lake is on your shoulder the whole way.

walks.n: Six Mile Creek / Mulholland Wildflower Preserve
walks.s: The city's own gorge: creek-level trail from Giles St up to the old dams and the reservoir, ten minutes from the Commons.
Three-quarters of a flat mile up the streambed to the base of the tallest single-drop waterfall in the northeast. Do it in October.
0.75 miles and 600 steps up past ten cascades — short, steep, and the closest big gorge hike to the city.

walks.n: Treman Gorge Trail to Lucifer Falls
walks.s: The county's best gorge walk: two and a half miles of hand-cut stone stairs and tunnels through a narrow gorge to a 115-foot fall.
Four miles of flat boardwalk and woods trails around a pond at the Lab of Ornithology — the best easy birding walk in the county, free, open dawn to dusk.
A rolling three-mile loop through 150 acres of collections above campus — drivable, walkable, and unbeatable in the third week of October.
A steep, unmanicured mile up to a 140-foot two-tier waterfall on the Finger Lakes Trail — the wildest falls hike near town.
Eight miles of crushed-stone rail trail from Cass Park to Taughannock Falls, flat the whole way — the county's best walk-or-ride out of town.
A gentle three-mile former rail bed climbing out of the city past Ithaca College — the flattest long walk on the south side.
Cornell's natural area on the Fall Creek flats — quiet loops through floodplain forest and the best cross-country ski track near campus.

museums.n: The History Center in Tompkins County
museums.s: Downtown local-history museum in the Tompkins Center for History and Culture — the room to visit before you walk the Commons.
The Johnson's fifth floor holds one of the strongest university Asian art collections in the US — Chinese bronzes and painting, with the valley through the window behind them.

museums.n: Cornell Fine Arts Library / Rare & Manuscript Collections
museums.s: The Kroch Library's rotating exhibitions from the rare books vault — Lincoln's Gettysburg Address draft, Wordsworth, the Hip Hop Collection. Free.
Ithaca College's contemporary gallery — small, sharp, free, and a reason to cross to South Hill.
Working print studio and gallery downtown — shows by member printmakers, plus classes you can drop into.

museums.n: Community School of Music and Arts
museums.s: CSMA's downtown building — three floors of studios and galleries, and the town's most consistent free show openings.
World-class glass museum an hour southwest — 50 centuries of objects, live hot-glass shows, and a make-your-own studio. The best rainy-Saturday drive from Ithaca.
Smithsonian-affiliate American art museum in downtown Corning — pair it with the glass museum and make a day of it.

shops.s: Ho Plaza's bookstore — textbooks, Big Red everything, a cafe, and the shipping counter you will end up needing.
A cooperatively owned bookstore on the Commons — the town's reading list, plus author nights most weeks.
Two floors of used books on the Commons, deep in scholarly leftovers from two campuses — the best used shelf between Syracuse and Binghamton.
In the basement under Autumn Leaves — a tight, well-curated vinyl room run by people who will actually talk to you about it.
Curated vintage on the Commons, decades deep and priced honestly — Ithaca's best-known clothing shop.
Used and consigned clothing on the Commons — the student-budget half of Ithaca's vintage scene.
Member-owned natural grocery with a hot bar, a good cheese counter and the west-end store that's bigger than you expect.
A restored service alley of tiny storefronts behind the Commons — coffee, books, a barber, a bottle shop, all in about 200 feet.
Guitars, amps and repairs in the DeWitt Mall — where every band in this town gets its strings.
Enormous nonprofit reuse warehouse on Elmira Rd — furniture, tools, books, and the place students furnish an apartment from in one trip.
Paper, pens and cards on the Commons — the shop for when you need a real card and not a text.
Sustainable housewares in the DeWitt Mall — the local answer for anything you'd otherwise order in a cardboard box.

essentials.s: The big Route 13 Wegmans — the default grocery run for anyone with a car, open late, with a pharmacy and a sub counter inside.
The campus health center on Ho Plaza — same-day care, pharmacy and after-hours phone triage for anyone with a Cornell ID.
The county hospital on the northwest hill — the emergency department for anything Cornell Health can't take.
Walk-in urgent care on Route 13 — stitches, X-rays and strep tests without the ER wait.
The 24-hour-ish Route 13 CVS — the prescription and cold-medicine fallback when campus is closed.
Upstate's own drugstore chain, on the west end — a friendlier pharmacy counter than the big two.
Route 13 farm-and-garden store — hardware, work boots, firewood, salt, and everything a rural county needs in November.
The big-box hardware store on Route 13 for anything Agway doesn't stock.
Big card-operated laundromat on the west end with wash-and-fold service — the fix when the dorm machines are all taken.
The main downtown branch on North Tioga — passports, packages, and the counter that actually knows how to ship a bike.
The county bus system, free with a Cornell ID on most routes — Route 30 and 10 connect campus, Collegetown and downtown all day.
24-hour gas and the late-night convenience stop on the Route 13 strip — the one that's always open on the way back from the trailhead.
New York-licensed adult-use cannabis dispensary in Ithaca — legal, tested product and a staff that will actually explain the menu.
West End bike and ski shop at 624 W State St doing full tune-ups and repairs — the fix after one Ithaca winter, and good Shindagin advice over the counter.
Card-operated laundromat in the Fall Creek neighborhood with wash-and-fold — the fix when every dorm machine is taken on a Sunday.

chinese.n: De Tasty Hot Pot 得味火锅
chinese.s: The Cornell hot pot institution — individual induction pots, a real Sichuan broth, and a mapo tofu and spicy fish stew that stand on their own. 15% service is added automatically.
The Szechuan kitchen Flushing expats grudgingly admit is good — order off the Chinese menu, skip the hot pot, and get the dry-fried string beans.
Small family-run Collegetown room that has fed Cornell for decades — the regional specials are the reason to come, not the sesame chicken.

chinese.n: Xi'an Street Food 西安小吃
chinese.s: Hand-pulled biang biang noodles and cumin lamb burgers done properly — the closest thing Ithaca has to a Xi'an Famous Foods.
Collegetown's late-night Chinese counter — the one open when everything else on College Ave has closed, and better than it has to be.
Numbing-hot Sichuan on the west end — the chili oil dishes and the cold appetizer case are where the kitchen shows off.

chinese.n: Ling Ling Kitchen 玲玲小厨
chinese.s: No-frills kitchen doing homestyle dishes for the Chinese student crowd — cheap, fast, and consistently the real thing.

chinese.n: Ren's Mart Asian Groceries 任家超市
chinese.s: Father-and-daughter Asian grocery on West Buffalo St — fresh greens, live seafood tanks, Sichuan pantry staples and the hot pot shopping list.

chinese.n: Win Li Supermarket 永利超市
chinese.s: The other Ithaca Asian market — broader Chinese and Korean dry goods, frozen dumplings and the noodle wall.

chinese.n: Green Castle Asian Market 翠堡
chinese.s: Small pan-Asian market near downtown — the quick stop for chili crisp, tofu and the one ingredient the other two are out of.
Locally made fresh tofu and soy products, sold at the farmers market and in local groceries — silken tofu worth planning a meal around.
Collegetown's boba counter and the default study-break run for the Chinese student community on College Ave.

chinese.n: Cornell East Asia Program at the Kahin Center
chinese.s: Cornell's East Asia Program runs public lectures, film nights and Chinese-language events out of the Kahin Center all term — free, and open to anyone.

fishing.s: The deep end of a 435-foot lake — lake trout and landlocked Atlantic salmon on the troll spring and fall, smallmouth and pike along the shallows.
The classic Finger Lakes tributary run: lake-run rainbows, browns and Atlantic salmon stack below the falls in spring and again in fall. 10.9 miles of public fishing rights upstream.
The inlet channel through the west end — rainbows in April, carp and pike in summer, and shore access the whole length of the flood-control channel.

fishing.n: Allan H. Treman Marine Park shoreline
fishing.s: Break wall, launch ramps and shoreline you can fish without a boat, right where the lake meets the inlet — the easy default after class.
Fifteen minutes up the east side: a waterfall pool and a run that fills with lake-run rainbows in spring and Atlantics in the fall.
The city's water supply above Ithaca — smallmouth, panfish and a quiet shoreline walk-in, with no boats to compete with.
Yes, you can fish the campus lake — bass, panfish and the occasional trout below Triphammer, five minutes from a lecture hall.
A shallow warmwater lake 20 minutes east — largemouth, pickerel and crappie, with a fishing pier and the rail trail around it.
The creek below the state park's falls — a short, steep tributary that gets a genuine spring rainbow run and almost no pressure.
Guided Cayuga Lake trips out of Ithaca — lake trout and salmon on downriggers, gear included, for when you want the deep water without a boat.

biking.s: Twenty miles of the best singletrack east of the Mississippi, ten miles east of campus — shale, roots, berms and long descents, maintained by Cycle-CNY.
Shindagin's north sibling — flowier, faster-drying, with a big loop network and a parking lot 20 minutes from campus.
The quieter third forest in the Dryden cluster — fewer people, more moss, and a good rainy-week alternative.
Steep, technical Finger Lakes Trail riding south of town — the climb is the point, and the descent is the reward.
Eight flat crushed-stone miles from Cass Park to Taughannock Falls — the gravel-bike and beginner ride, with the lake alongside.
A quiet four-mile rail trail through Dryden past the lake — a flat spin when the forests are too wet to ride.
The student club runs road and mountain group rides out of campus all term — the fastest way to find the good lines at Shindagin.

social.s: 160 vendors under a lakeside pavilion at Steamboat Landing, all from within 30 miles — produce, crafts and a food row worth going hungry for.
Salsa Ithaca's weekly Latin night — a lesson first, then salsa, bachata and Cuban casino until late. No partner needed, all levels.
Salsa Ithaca's weekly Afro-Cuban class with live percussion — the most joyful room in the county on a Tuesday.

social.n: West Coast Swing at Seven of Jazz
social.s: Weekly West Coast swing lesson and social at the Seven of Jazz Lounge on South Cayuga — beginners taught first, then dancing.
Ithaca's contra dance crew — live band, called every dance, no partner and no experience required. The friendliest way to meet 60 people in one night.
Lindy and balboa socials run by the local swing network, with a beginner lesson before each — venues rotate, the crowd doesn't.
Downtown's Monday trivia — two floors, a full bar, and a quiz that draws grad students who take it far too seriously.
Early-evening live jazz in the Argos Inn's front room every Wednesday — free, no cover, and the best-dressed hour in Ithaca.
Student chimesmasters play the 21 bells three times every weekday — climb the tower and watch from inside the bell chamber.
Downtown galleries and studios open late together on the second Saturday — free, walkable, and the easiest low-pressure evening out.

social.n: Finger Lakes Runners Club group runs
social.s: The county running club's weekly no-drop group runs from rotating trailheads — the fastest way into the local trail scene on foot.
Willard Straight's repertory program — 35mm classics, new international releases and director visits, several nights a week during term.

social.n: Ithaca Beer Co. run & trivia nights
social.s: The taproom's weekday programming — a group run out the Black Diamond and trivia on the lawn when the weather holds.
